summary: Iman Makaremi from Cat.io discusses building an AI copilot for enterprise cloud architects using multi-agent orchestration. The motivation is that cloud architecture requires reasoning—not just automation—because architects negotiate trade-offs among requirements, time, and resources using scattered, implicit context. Cat.io identifies three core challenges: requirement understanding, architecture identification, and architecture recommendation. The fundamental AI challenge is bridging semantic/textual requirement documents with inherently graph-based architecture data. For grounding, they tried semantic enrichment of architecture components for vector search, graph-enhanced component search using graph algorithms, and early-score enrichment of requirement documents using requirement templates called pods. They learned semantic grounding improves reasoning but doesn't always scale, and graph memory supports continuity beyond accuracy. For complex reasoning, they built multi-agent orchestration with role-specific agents: one chief architect overseeing higher-level tasks, ten staff architects each specialized in domains like infrastructure and API, and two retrievers (requirement and architecture). The workflow has three sequential tasks: list generation, conflict resolution where the chief architect prunes redundant or conflicting recommendations, and design proposal generation. Staff architects send parallel requests to retrievers, with calls happening multiple times based on budgets. Agent cloning occurs during design proposal generation—each staff architect is cloned per recommendation, with clones accessing past history but maintaining separate current history. Key design choices include structured message formats, isolated context management to reduce hallucination, and explicit control flows. For evaluation, LLM evaluations were insufficient, so they built an internal human eval tool called Eagle Eye for examining architecture, requirements, agent conversations, and recommendations with relevance, visibility, and clarity scoring. Key learnings: confidence is not correctness, human feedback is essential early on, and evaluation must be baked into system design from the start. Makaremi concludes that building a copilot is about designing a reasoning system, not just generating answers. Graphs are becoming increasingly important, and they are moving toward LangGraph for agent workflows with a manager on top, Flyte for higher-level management, and graphs for capturing memory and context. The recommendation system is in production.
whyItMatters: The talk connects its engineering abstractions, implementation choices, and AI/product implications into one practical system view.

sections.title: Motivation: Cloud Architecture Needs Reasoning
sections.summary: Makaremi introduces the talk, explaining that cloud architecture requires reasoning beyond automation due to growing system complexity, diverse tools, and rising expectations. Architects negotiate trade-offs using scattered implicit context, and AI must understand how architects think.

sections.title: Three Core Challenges: Requirements, Identification, Recommendations
sections.summary: Cat.io identifies three challenges: requirement understanding (sources, formats, importance), architecture identification (component functions), and architecture recommendation. The AI challenge involves mixing semantic text with graph-based architecture data, handling complex vague questions, and evaluating feedback.

sections.title: Grounding Agents in Architecture Context
sections.summary: Describes approaches to grounding: semantic enrichment of architecture components for vector search, graph-enhanced component search using graph algorithms, and early-score enrichment of requirement documents. Learnings: semantic grounding helps but doesn't always scale, proper design is critical, and graph memory supports continuity not just accuracy.

sections.title: Architecture Retrieval Design and Graph-Based Evolution
sections.summary: Shows early architecture retrieval design: breaking architecture into components, converting JSON to natural language, enriching with connection data, and vector embedding. Found semantic search has limitations for graph data, prompting evolution toward knowledge graph-based searches.

sections.title: Requirement Understanding with Templates
sections.summary: Describes requirement document processing using requirement templates ('pods') to structure extracted information. This enabled fast retrieval and structured business requirements, but context was lost as document volume increased, suggesting graph analysis could help.

sections.title: Complex Reasoning with Multi-Agent Orchestration
sections.summary: Covers multi-agent orchestration with role-specific agents that collaborate, argue, and converge on justified recommendations. Key design choices: structured message formats (evolved from XML), isolated context management to save tokens and reduce hallucination, agent cloning for parallel processing, structured outputs despite reasoning trade-offs, and the necessity of explicit control flows. Recommendation system is in production.

sections.title: Multi-Agent Workflow and Recommendation Pipeline
sections.summary: Details the multi-agent system: one chief architect overseeing higher-level tasks, ten staff architects specialized in domains like infrastructure and API, and two retrievers (requirement and architecture). The workflow has three sequential tasks: list generation, conflict resolution where the chief architect prunes conflicts and redundancies, and design proposal generation. Staff architects send parallel requests to retrievers based on budgets. Agent cloning occurs during design proposals—each staff architect is cloned per recommendation, with clones accessing past history but maintaining separate current history.

sections.title: Evaluation, Feedback, and Human Scoring
sections.summary: Covers evaluation challenges in multi-agent systems with many agents and rounds of conversations. They closed the loop with human scoring and structured feedback/revision cycles. LLM evaluations were insufficient for needed improvements, so they built Eagle Eye, an internal human eval tool for examining architecture, requirements, agent conversations, and recommendations with relevance, visibility, and clarity scoring. Key learnings: confidence is not correctness, human feedback is essential early on, and evaluation must be baked into system design from the start. Shows a hallucination example where a staff architect asked a requirements retriever to schedule a workshop.

sections.title: Conclusions: Reasoning Systems and Future Directions
sections.summary: Concludes that building a copilot is about designing a reasoning system, not just generating answers. The system needs roles, workflows, memories, and structure to handle large data (thousands or millions of components). Graphs are becoming increasingly important in designs. They are moving toward LangGraph for agent workflows with a manager on top, Flyte for higher-level management, and graphs for capturing memory and context. They believe this represents how AI will design software.
